prediction_made_before_the_data: Nothing below five minutes, rising through the band, gone again past an hour.

what_the_data_says.confirmed: The cliff at five minutes. Two schedules below it -- interactive at ~7s and a two-minute timer -- put 0 of 26 and 0 of 30 gaps in the band and recovered nothing. Three above it recovered 13-17%. That boundary is sharp, reproducible, and is where the default TTL starts costing money.
what_the_data_says.refuted: The rise. 420s, 600s and 900s came back 14%, 17% and 13% -- a 4-point spread on samples of about twenty requests each, which is noise. The shape inside the band is not resolved by this data and the earlier 17% should not be read as a peak.
what_the_data_says.untested: The far side. No schedule beyond an hour was run, so the prediction that the saving disappears again past 3600s is arithmetic, not measurement.

honest_claim: For this agent and this task: a schedule slower than five minutes makes roughly 13-17% of input spend recoverable by moving to a one-hour TTL; a schedule faster than five minutes makes none. The threshold transfers because it is a property of the five-minute lifetime. The magnitude is one agent, one task, one model, and should be measured per workload rather than quoted.
